questions.question_text:
In the proof that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\log_{a}x)=\dfrac{1}{x\ln a}$, we write $\log_{a}x=\dfrac{1}{\ln a}\times\ln x$.
Why can $\dfrac{1}{\ln a}$ be taken outside the differentiation?

options.text: Because $a$ is a constant, $\ln a$ is a fixed number, so $\dfrac{1}{\ln a}$ is a constant multiplier.
Because $\ln a$ cancels with the $\ln x$ in the numerator.
options.why: Cancels a whole logarithm out of a quotient, which is not a valid log law.

options.text: Because the derivative of every logarithm is $\dfrac{1}{x}$, so the base never matters.
options.why: Ignores the base entirely, but the base scales the derivative by the factor $\dfrac{1}{\ln a}$.

options.text: Because $\ln a$ depends on $x$ and must be handled by the chain rule.
options.why: Treats the constant base $a$ as though it varied with $x$.

questions.solution_text:
$\log_{a}x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln a}=\dfrac{1}{\ln a}\times\ln x$
The base $a$ is a constant, so $\ln a$ is a fixed number and $\dfrac{1}{\ln a}$ is a constant multiplier.
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\log_{a}x)=\dfrac{1}{\ln a}\times\dfrac{1}{x}$
$=\dfrac{1}{x\ln a}$
